newsitem.title: UK: AMBIENT MEDIA - AD AGENCIES USE UNCONVENTIONAL METHODS TO REACH CUSTOMER.
newsitem.headline: AMBIENT MEDIA - AD AGENCIES USE UNCONVENTIONAL METHODS TO REACH CUSTOMER.

text.p: Toilet walls, golf holes and even cows are being used as advertising sites by agencies trying to reach jaded consumers.
Since a growing number of Westerners are ignoring ads on posters, in print and on television, companies are going to unusual and sometimes bizarre lengths to get consumers' attention.
They are running ads on everything from bus and tube tickets to petrol pump nozzles to the lids of takeaway meals -- and even on eggs.
British company Egg-Vert UK has printed ads on more than 30 million eggs for companies including British Telecommunications Plc and Channel 4.
"Advertisers will try almost anything to grab people's attention," Shaun McIlrath, creative director of the London-based advertising agency Impact FCA, told Reuters.
"Consumers are becoming increasingly difficult to reach. Conventional advertising mediums are saturated and agencies have to be much more inventive to break through the clutter."
AMBIENT MEDIA
Industry experts estimate that the market in Britain for ads in unconventional places or so-called "ambient media" is worth 10 million ($16 million).

London's famous black taxis were among the first "ambient media" sites to be introduced and are covered with advertisements for chocolate bars, newspapers and airlines. About 5,000 of the 18,000 taxis licensed to work in greater London carry ads on the outside.

Brian Jones, a London taxi driver who has his cab sprayed bright green with an ad for "Snickers" chocolate bars, said:"I quite like the ad although I don't know if anyone who sees my cab thinks I fancy a Snickers".

In Spain, media company SPM Logocar is paying private citizens 30,000 pesetas ($210) to allow their cars to be covered in customised vinyl stickers promoting corporate brands, the Wall Street Journal Europe reported recently.
The company also hopes to attract mobile phone companies, pizza restaurants and soft drinks firms.
In London, taxi advertising has now gone a step further with a campaign for Siemens mobile phones in which taxi drivers are paid to tell passengers about the product.

Impact FCA's McIlrath, who is the brains behind the campaign said :"We expect to reach 2,500 consumers this way and it is a much more direct form of advertising than just hoping that people will look at a poster or a TV ad."
OTHER UNUSUAL SITES
It's not just London cabs which have become temporary advertising sites -- some of the city's most famous landmarks have carried ads.

Confectioner Cadbury Schweppes Plc last year arranged for an image of its Whispa Gold chocolate brand to be laser projected onto the dome of St Paul's Cathedral. The company paid a substantial sum to the cathedral's restoration fund in return for permission to use the dome for five hours.
As well as providing grand gestures, "ambient media" is also a way of targeting particular groups of consumers.
Upmarket male consumers are being targeted on golf courses where media company Golf Media places ads in golf holes for products such as malt whisky and cars.
"Consumers have 18 chances to see the ads," said a company spokesman.
Car owners are targeted through ads on petrol pump nozzles.

"We have a captive audience because there is very little else to look at during the time it takes to fill up a car," said Kim Cross, a director of sales house Multiple Listing Services, which handles petrol pump advertising.
"One of our clients, an insurance company, says it has had a 60 percent uplift in enquiries since it began using this form of media."
Other ads are appearing on London underground tickets and phone cards that are used in many of the city's public telephones.
Even the most intimate moments are not immune to the hard sell.
A number of companies around the world advertise travel sickness remedies on airline sick bags that are tucked into the pouch behind seats on international carriers.
And Manchester-based Hi Tech Solutions, which specialises in targeting the youth market, has introduced advertising on toilet walls in pubs and night-clubs across Britain.

"It's pretty radical but we are tapping into a captive audience. We estimate that consumers spend on average 30 seconds in there looking at an ad 15 inches from their faces," said Richard Weir sales and marketing director.
He added that if consumers are drinking heavily then they will have the chance to see the ad not just once but four or five times in the course of an evening.
Companies that are using toilet advertising include IDV for its Jose Cuervo Gold tequila brand and Virgin for its video games.
Innovative advertising sites not only attract consumer attention but can generate media exposure that helps the company which is selling the goods or services.
One example was a campaign devised by a public relations company, Ocean Blue, for its Internet client MarketingNet.
Ocean Blue persuaded a British farmer to dress his cows in jackets bearing the MarketingNet name.

"We got our client world-wide media coverage. We used eight cows wearing the jackets and paid the farmer 250 pounds ($407) per cow. The media coverage was tremendous and you couldn't buy that amount of exposure," said Richard Strange, a spokesman for the company.
Ad agency TBWA is also a fan of "ambient media". It laser projected a 50-foot (15-metre)-high image of supermodel Eva Herzigova wearing a "Wonderbra" onto the Battersea Power Station in London.

"The initial spend was 200,000 pounds but we estimate we have had 60 million pounds worth of free media coverage as a result", said TBWA's chairman Jo Hoare. ($ = 142.6 Spanish Pesetas) ($ = 0.614 British Pounds Sterling)
